slot.brief: Arrange given Group 16 hydrides by boiling point / thermal stability or Group 13 oxides by acidity, testing anomalous trends.

stem: Which of the following represents the correct increasing order of boiling points for the hydrides $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{PH}_3$, $\text{AsH}_3$, and $\text{SbH}_3$?

verdicts.working: Actual boiling points: PH3 185.4 K (−87.7 °C) < AsH3 210.6 K (−62.5 °C) < NH3 239.7 K (−33.4 °C) < SbH3 254.6 K (−18.5 °C). NH3 is elevated by H-bonding above PH3 and AsH3, but SbH3's large van der Waals forces push it above NH3. Order matches option C.

working:
The boiling point of covalent hydrides generally increases down a group due to increasing molecular mass and surface area, which enhances London dispersion (van der Waals) forces: $\text{PH}_3 < \text{AsH}_3 < \text{SbH}_3$. However, $\text{NH}_3$ exhibits intermolecular hydrogen bonding due to the high electronegativity and small size of nitrogen, giving it an anomalously high boiling point compared to $\text{PH}_3$ and $\text{AsH}_3$. In $\text{SbH}_3$, the molecular mass is large enough that the strong van der Waals attractions outweigh the hydrogen bonding present in $\text{NH}_3$. Experimental boiling points (from NCERT): $\text{PH}_3\ (185.5\ \text{K}) < \text{AsH}_3\ (210.6\ \text{K}) < \text{NH}_3\ (238.5\ \text{K}) < \text{SbH}_3\ (254.6\ \text{K})$. Therefore, the correct order is $\text{PH}_3 < \text{AsH}_3 < \text{NH}_3 < \text{SbH}_3$.

Independent check: Actual boiling points: PH3 185.4 K (−87.7 °C) < AsH3 210.6 K (−62.5 °C) < NH3 239.7 K (−33.4 °C) < SbH3 254.6 K (−18.5 °C). NH3 is elevated by H-bonding above PH3 and AsH3, but SbH3's large van der Waals forces push it above NH3. Order matches option C.
